claim: AMPARs control fast synaptic communication between neurons and their function relies on auxiliary subunits, which importantly modulate channel properties.
source: AMPARs control fast synaptic communication between neurons and their function relies on auxiliary subunits, which importantly modulate channel properties.
evidence: This is a general statement about AMPAR function that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: AMPARs can bind to TARPs with variable stoichiometry.
source: Although it has been suggested that AMPARs can bind to TARPs with variable stoichiometry, little is known about the effect that this stoichiometry exerts on certain AMPAR properties.
evidence: The statement indicates this has been suggested in prior work, implying citation-based support.

claim: AMPARs show a clear stoichiometry-dependent modulation by the prototypical TARP γ2.
source: Here we have found that AMPARs show a clear stoichiometry-dependent modulation by the prototypical TARP γ2 although the receptor still needs to be fully saturated with γ2 to show some typical TARP-induced characteristics (i.e. an increase in channel conductance).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The receptor needs to be fully saturated with γ2 to show an increase in channel conductance.
source: Here we have found that AMPARs show a clear stoichiometry-dependent modulation by the prototypical TARP γ2 although the receptor still needs to be fully saturated with γ2 to show some typical TARP-induced characteristics (i.e. an increase in channel conductance).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: There are important differences in the stoichiometric modulation between calcium-permeable and calcium-impermeable AMPARs.
source: We also uncovered important differences in the stoichiometric modulation between calcium-permeable and calcium-impermeable AMPARs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: In heteromeric AMPARs, γ2 positioning in the complex is important to exert certain TARP-dependent features.
source: Moreover, in heteromeric AMPARs, γ2 positioning in the complex is important to exert certain TARP-dependent features.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: There is a likely presence of two γ2 molecules at somatic receptors in cerebellar granule cells.
source: Finally, by comparing data from recombinant receptors with endogenous AMPAR currents from mouse cerebellar granule cells, we have determined a likely presence of two γ2 molecules at somatic receptors in this cell type.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing experimental data from recombinant systems with native neurons.

claim: Glutamate is a crucial neurotransmitter in the central nervous system (CNS), mediating the vast majority of the fast-excitatory synaptic transmission acting on postsynaptic ionotropic glutamate receptors.
source: Glutamate is a crucial neurotransmitter in the central nervous system (CNS), mediating the vast majority of the fast-excitatory synaptic transmission acting on postsynaptic ionotropic glutamate receptors.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about glutamate function.

claim: AMPARs are fundamental players in the synaptic course besides their pivotal role as regulators of synaptic plasticity.
source: Among these, α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptors (AMPARs) are fundamental players in the synaptic course besides their pivotal role as regulators of synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AMPAR function.

claim: AMPARs are homo or heterotetrameric structures composed of four GluA subunits (GluA1-4).
source: AMPARs are homo or heterotetrameric structures composed of four GluA subunits (GluA1-4) (Traynelis et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The presence or absence of the GluA2 subunit is a critical determinant of AMPAR channel behaviour.
source: their biophysical properties are dramatically changed depending on the subunits that conform the ion channel, with the presence or absence of the GluA2 subunit a critical determinant of channel behaviour.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AMPAR subunit composition effects.

claim: GluA2-lacking AMPARs are permeable to both Na+ and Ca2+ ions.
source: In particular, while GluA2-lacking AMPARs are permeable to both Na+ and Ca2+ ions, AMPARs containing the GluA2 subunit are impermeable to Ca2+.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AMPAR permeability properties.

claim: AMPARs containing the GluA2 subunit are impermeable to Ca2+.
source: In particular, while GluA2-lacking AMPARs are permeable to both Na+ and Ca2+ ions, AMPARs containing the GluA2 subunit are impermeable to Ca2+.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AMPAR permeability properties.

claim: GluA2-containing AMPARs do not allow Ca2+ influx through the channel due to an RNA editing process that results in the replacement of a neutral glutamine for the positive amino acid arginine in the cation selectivity filter region of this subunit at the so-called Q/R site.
source: GluA2-containing AMPARs do not allow Ca2+ influx through the channel due to an RNA editing process that results in the replacement of a neutral glutamine for the positive amino acid arginine in the cation selectivity filter region of this subunit at the so-called Q/R site (Hollmann et al., 1991; Burnashev et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: GluA2-exclusive RNA editing process occurs in 99% of native GluA2 subunits.
source: GluA2-exclusive RNA editing process occurs in 99% of native GluA2 subunits (Geiger et al., 1995; Kawahara et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Q/R editing affects Ca2+ permeability and single-channel conductance, which is decreased in GluA2-containing AMPARs mainly due to the lack of Ca2+ permeability.
source: This change not only affects Ca2+ permeability but also single-channel conductance, which is decreased in GluA2-containing AMPARs mainly due to the lack of Ca2+ permeability (Swanson et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Editing at the Q/R site impairs the blocking effect of endogenous polyamines on these receptors at depolarized membrane potentials compared to GluA2-lacking AMPARs, which are strongly blocked by spermine.
source: Editing at the Q/R site also impairs the blocking effect of endogenous polyamines on these receptors at depolarized membrane potentials compared to GluA2-lacking AMPARs, which are strongly blocked by spermine (Bowie and Mayer, 1995; Kamboj et al., 1995; Koh et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Q/R editing of the GluA2 subunit powerfully influences AMPAR tetramerization and strongly disfavours formation of GluA2 homotetramers.
source: Finally, the Q/R editing of the GluA2 subunit powerfully influences AMPAR tetramerization and strongly disfavours formation of GluA2 homotetramers (Greger et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A marginal population of GluA2 homomers (~1%) have been found to reach the plasma membrane in vivo.
source: although a marginal population of GluA2 homomers (~1%) have been found to reach the plasma membrane in vivo (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: AMPAR gating and trafficking properties are determined by their subunit composition.
source: While AMPAR gating – and also trafficking – properties are determined by their subunit composition, these features are also strongly dependent on AMPAR-associated transmembrane proteins that behave as auxiliary subunits of the receptor.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AMPAR regulation.

claim: AMPAR features are strongly dependent on AMPAR-associated transmembrane proteins that behave as auxiliary subunits of the receptor.
source: While AMPAR gating – and also trafficking – properties are determined by their subunit composition, these features are also strongly dependent on AMPAR-associated transmembrane proteins that behave as auxiliary subunits of the receptor.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AMPAR regulation.

claim: In the last 15 years, the number of interacting proteins that can act as modulatory partners of AMPARs has vastly increased.
source: In the last 15 years, the number of interacting proteins that can act as modulatory partners of AMPARs has vastly increased.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field's progress over time.

claim: Stargazin and other TARPs were the first AMPAR-modulating proteins to be discovered.
source: Stargazin and other TARPs (Transmembrane AMPAR Regulatory Proteins) were the first AMPAR-modulating proteins to be discovered (Chen et al., 2000; Tomita et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TARPs play an indispensable role in neuronal physiology and in different types of synaptic plasticity.
source: TARPs are one of the most studied AMPAR auxiliary proteins because of their indispensable role in neuronal physiology (see Payne, 2008 for review) and in different types of synaptic plasticity (Rouach et al., 2005; Louros et al., 2014; Sullivan et al., 2017; Louros et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Members of the TARP family can modify biophysical properties of AMPARs by increasing conductance, slowing down kinetics or diminishing polyamine block in CP-AMPARs.
source: It is well-known that members of the TARP family can modify biophysical properties of AMPARs by increasing conductance, slowing down kinetics or diminishing polyamine block in CP-AMPARs (Straub and Tomita, 2012; Haering et al., 2014; Jackson and Nicoll, 2011; Greger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TARPs can modify AMPAR pharmacology such as kainate-evoked responses.
source: Furthermore, TARPs can modify AMPAR pharmacology such as kainate-evoked responses (Turetsky et al., 2005; Kott et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: AMPAR/TARP stoichiometry has been investigated by single-molecule subunit counting.
source: However, much less is known about the number of TARP molecules that can be present in an AMPAR complex although AMPAR/TARP stoichiometry has been investigated by single-molecule subunit counting (Hastie et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Electrophysiological studies demonstrated that AMPAR efficiency to kainate varies depending on the number of TARPs present in the receptor.
source: and electrophysiological studies, which demonstrated that AMPAR efficiency to kainate varies depending on the number of TARPs present in the receptor (Shi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Functional studies together with high definition structural data provided evidence for a favoured 2-TARP per AMPAR stoichiometry.
source: More recently, functional studies together with high definition structural data provided evidence for a favoured 2-TARP per AMPAR stoichiometry (Dawe et al., 2019; Herguedas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: It is still not established whether TARPs can modulate AMPARs in a stoichiometry dependent manner.
source: However, with only a small number of studies investigating AMPAR/TARP stoichiometry, it is still not established whether TARPs can modulate AMPARs in a stoichiometry dependent manner.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The number of γ2 per AMPAR complex modifies the biophysical properties of these receptors in a stoichiometry dependent manner in both CP and CI-AMPARs.
source: In the present work we have determined how the number of γ2 (the prototypical TARP) per AMPAR complex modifies the biophysical properties of these receptors in a stoichiometry dependent manner in both CP and CI-AMPARs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: AMPAR/TARP fusion proteins were used to fix stoichiometries of 2 and 4 TARPs per AMPAR.
source: To approach this issue, we have used AMPAR/TARP fusion proteins to fix stoichiometries of 2 and 4 TARPs per AMPAR.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: There are important differences observed between CP and CI-AMPARs in stoichiometry-dependent modulation.
source: Our results show a complex stoichiometry-dependent modulation with important differences observed between CP and CI-AMPARs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Cerebellar granule cells express a limited variety of GluA and TARP subunits together with a lack of cornichons expression on the plasma membrane.
source: We have taken advantage that this cerebellar neuronal type expresses a limited variety of GluA and TARP subunits together with a lack of cornichons expression on the plasma membrane (another important AMPAR auxiliary protein) (Schwenk et al., 2009; Shi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Just 2 molecules of the TARP family (specifically γ2) determine functional somatic AMPAR properties in CGCs acting in a complex manner on both GluA2 and GluA4c subunits.
source: We propose that just 2 molecules of the TARP family (specifically γ2) determine functional somatic AMPAR properties in CGCs acting in a complex manner on both GluA2 and GluA4c subunits.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's experimental data.

claim: The archetypal TARP γ2 slows deactivation and desensitization of AMPAR-mediated responses.
source: The archetypal TARP γ2 slows deactivation and desensitization of AMPAR-mediated responses (Priel et al., 2005), as observed with the other members of the TARP family (Soto et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A significant change in steady state current was detected when the CP-AMPAR was fully saturated with TARPs.
source: A significant change was detected when the CP-AMPAR was fully saturated with TARPs (2.78 ± 1.04% for 0-TARPs vs. 13.95 ± 1.85% for 4-TARPs; p<0.001; one-way ANOVA)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Rise time of the current activation was not significantly increased by TARPs.
source: We next analysed the kinetics of the current activation (rise time) and we did not observe a significant increase in the time to reach the peak current (0.46 ± 0.06 ms, 0.61 ± 0.12 ms and 0.67 ± 0.08 ms for 0-TARPs, 2-TARPs and 4-TARPs respectively; one-way ANOVA; p>0.05 for all comparisons between groups; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: TARPs speed the recovery from desensitization of AMPARs.
source: TARPs also speed the recovery from desensitization of AMPARs (Priel et al., 2005; Gill et al., 2012; Cais et al., 2014; Carbone and Plested, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Desensitization recovery rate showed a graded effect, with the 2-TARPs condition halfway between the slow recovery of 0-TARPs and the quicker recovery of 4-TARPs.
source: We then calculated the desensitization recovery rate and we observed a graded effect, with the 2-TARPs condition halfway between the slow recovery of 0-TARPs and the quicker recovery of 4-TARPs (Figure 2B). Specifically, we found time constants (τ) of 98.57 ± 7.35 ms for 0-TARPs, 68.91 ± 5.92 ms for 2-TARPs and 53.86 ± 4.78 ms for 4-TARPs (Figure 2C; n = 9, 14 and 10 respectively).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: CP-AMPARs show a strong intracellular polyamine block of the channel especially at depolarized potentials, which translates into a characteristic inwardly rectifying current-voltage relationship.
source: An important canonical property of CP-AMPARs is the strong intracellular polyamine block of the channel especially at depolarized potentials, which translates into a characteristic inwardly rectifying current-voltage relationship (Kamboj et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The strong polyamine block is attenuated as a consequence of TARP modulation.
source: This strong block by polyamines is attenuated as a consequence of TARP modulation (Soto et al., 2007; Soto et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A strong dependence on the number of γ2 molecules associated with the CP-AMPAR in attenuation of spermine block across different membrane voltages was observed.
source: A strong dependence on the number of γ2 molecules associated with the CP-AMPAR in such attenuation across different membrane voltages was observed (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The rectification index clearly demonstrates a stoichiometry dependence of γ2-mediated attenuation of spermine block.
source: The rectification index (RI; +60 mV /-60 mV; Figure 3C) clearly demonstrates a stoichiometry dependence of γ2-mediated attenuation of spermine block (0.056 ± 0.004 for 0-TARPs; 0.128 ± 0.011 for 2-TARPs and 0.274 ± 0.021 for 4-TARPs; p<0.05 for comparisons between all groups; one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: 80% of the responses from GluA1(Q) and GluA1(R) co-transfection showed a RI >0.7.
source: We found that 80% of the responses showed a RI >0.7 (8 out of 10 recordings).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data.

claim: When GluA1(Q):γ2 was co-transfected with GluA1(R), RIs above 0.7 were observed in all recorded patches.
source: When we co-transfected GluA1(Q):γ2 with GluA1(R) we observed RIs above 0.7 in all recorded patches (n = 9), a percentage that did not differ from the TARPless condition (p=0.4737; Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data.

claim: The weighted time constant (τw) of the TARPed GluA1(R)-containing receptor was slowed significantly compared with the TARPless receptor.
source: Importantly, as detected with GluA1(Q) forms, in the GluA1(R)-containing receptors the weighted time constant (τw) of the TARPed receptor was slowed significantly compared with the TARPless receptor (2.87 ± 0.47 for 0-TARPs vs. 4.32 ± 0.46 for 2-TARPs; p<0.05; student's t-test; data not shown).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data.

claim: The results obtained in the 2-TARPed conditions with GluA1(Q) were acquired putatively from a major 2-TARPed population.
source: This suggests that the results obtained in the 2-TARPed conditions with GluA1(Q) from Figures 1–3 were acquired putatively from a major 2-TARPed population, although it cannot be completely ruled out the presence of a small amount of 'contaminating' homomeric AMPARs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Conductance values for TARPless GluA1 homomeric receptors were 16.58 ± 0.69 pS.
source: We obtained conductance values for TARPless GluA1 homomeric receptors (16.58 ± 0.69 pS; Figure 4C) similar to conductance values of 16.53 pS we previously described in the laboratory (Gratacòs-Batlle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: GluA1:γ2 fusion protein (4-TARPed) responses were increased ∼1.4–1.5 fold as previously described when GluA1 is co-transfected together with γ2.
source: As expected GluA1:γ2 fusion protein (4-TARPed) responses were increased ∼1.4–1.5 fold as previously described when GluA1 is co-transfected together with γ2 (Soto et al., 2014) (16.58 ± 0.69 pS for 0-TARP vs. 24.34 ± 1.69 pS for 4-TARP; p<0.01; n = 10 and 16 respectively; Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 4, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The 2-TARP condition (co-transfection of GluA1 and GluA1:γ2) did not increase single-channel conductance.
source: Surprisingly, the 2-TARP condition (co-transfection of GluA1 and GluA1:γ2) did not increase single-channel conductance (16.58 ± 0.69 pS for 0-TARP vs. 17.03 ± 2.06 pS for 2-TARP; p>0.05; n = 10 for both conditions), indicating that 2 γ2 molecules were not sufficient to increase AMPAR conductance.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data.

claim: 2 γ2 molecules were not sufficient to increase AMPAR conductance.
source: Surprisingly, the 2-TARP condition (co-transfection of GluA1 and GluA1:γ2) did not increase single-channel conductance (16.58 ± 0.69 pS for 0-TARP vs. 17.03 ± 2.06 pS for 2-TARP; p>0.05; n = 10 for both conditions), indicating that 2 γ2 molecules were not sufficient to increase AMPAR conductance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Some studies have shown an increase of open probability in AMPARs mediated by γ2.
source: Some studies have shown an increase of open probability in AMPARs mediated by γ2 (Suzuki et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Other studies have not observed an increase in open probability with γ2 nor with other members of the TARP I subfamily.
source: while others have not observed such an increase with γ2 nor with other members of the TARP I subfamily (Soto et al., 2007; Shi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: No increase of Po,peak was found regardless of the amount of γ2 in the AMPAR complex.
source: As shown in Figure 4D, we did not find any increase of Po,peak regardless of the amount of γ2 in the AMPAR complex (0.54 ± 0.06, 0.47 ± 0.06 and 0.62 ± 0.05 for 0-TARPs, 2-TARPs and 4-TARPs. p>0.05 for all comparisons between groups. One-way ANOVA; n = 9,10 and 17 respectively).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: An alternative splicing short isoform of GluA4 – GluA4c – is highly expressed in CGCs.
source: However, an alternative splicing short isoform of GluA4 – GluA4c – is highly expressed in CGCs (Gallo et al., 1992; Kawahara et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: GluA4c homomeric AMPARs were functionally identical to GluA4 homomers.
source: When long and short forms of GluA4 were compared we observed that GluA4c homomeric AMPARs were functionally identical to GluA4 homomers.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data.

claim: No differences were spotted in the single channel conductance or peak open probability between GluA4 and GluA4c.
source: No differences were spotted in the single channel conductance or peak open probability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B) measured by means of NSFA.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Desensitization kinetics did not differ between GluA4 and GluA4c isoforms.
source: Likewise, desensitization kinetics did not differ between both isoforms (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both GluA4 and GluA4c homomeric receptors presented the same degree of intracellular block by spermine.
source: Finally, both homomeric receptors presented the same degree of intracellular block by spermine (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Any number of γ2 molecules into the CI-AMPAR was sufficient to increase single channel conductance.
source: Although any number of γ2 molecules into the CI-AMPAR was sufficient to increase single channel conductance as reported previously (Jackson et al., 2011) (p<0.01 for all comparisons between 0-TARPs and the other TARPed groups; Figure 5C–D), the γ2 location within the complex was important in determining the extent of conductance increase.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 5, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The γ2 location within the CI-AMPAR complex was important in determining the extent of conductance increase.
source: Although any number of γ2 molecules into the CI-AMPAR was sufficient to increase single channel conductance as reported previously (Jackson et al., 2011) (p<0.01 for all comparisons between 0-TARPs and the other TARPed groups; Figure 5C–D), the γ2 location within the complex was important in determining the extent of conductance increase.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: γ2 intensified its effect on single channel conductance when it was attached to GluA2 subunit compared with GluA4c.
source: Specifically, γ2 intensified its effect on single channel conductance when it was attached to GluA2 subunit compared with GluA4c (15.85 ± 1.62 pS vs. 9.72 ± 1.09 pS for γ2 attached to GluA2 or GluA4c respectively; p<0.01; n = 10 and 20 patches), which represents a 309% and an 189% conductance increase respect to GluA2/GluA4c (5.13 ± 0.50 pS).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data.

claim: Peak open probability deduced from NSFA did not seem to be affected regardless of the number of TARP molecules or their location on GluA2-containing heteromers.
source: Finally, peak open probability deduced from the same NSFA did not seem to be affected regardless of the number of TARP molecules or their location on GluA2-containing heteromers (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Desensitization kinetics of GluA2/GluA4c heteromeric combination were slowed down only when γ2 was linked to GluA4c subunit irrespective of a 2- or 4-TARP stoichiometry.
source: Figure 6A–B shows that desensitization kinetics of GluA2/GluA4c heteromeric combination (0T) were slowed down only when γ2 was linked to GluA4c subunit irrespective of a 2- or 4-TARP stoichiometry.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The kinetics of GluA2/GluA4c:γ2 were not different from GluA2:γ2/GluA4c:γ2.
source: Indeed, the kinetics of GluA2/GluA4c:γ2 – 2T(A4c) – were not different from GluA2:γ2/GluA4c:γ2–4T – (7.23 ± 0.43 ms for 2T(A4c) vs. 8.43 ± 0.61 ms for 4T; p>0.05; n = 21 and 20 respectively; Figure 6C)
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: γ2 linked to GluA2 subunits did not seem to affect GluA2/GluA4c desensitization.
source: Finally, γ2 linked to GluA2 subunits did not seem to affect GluA2/GluA4c desensitization (4.76 ± 0.28 ms for 0T vs. 5.42 ± 0.40 ms for 2T(A2); p>0.05; n = 14 and 11, respectively).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data.

claim: Kinetic behaviour in CI-AMPARs is apparently not changed by γ2 unless the TARP is attached to GluA4c subunit.
source: Thus, kinetic behaviour in CI-AMPARs is apparently not changed by γ2 unless the TARP is attached to GluA4c subunit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: No variation in rise time was noticed amongst the different CI-AMPAR combinations tested.
source: Concerning the activation time to reach the peak current (rise time), we did not notice any variation amongst the different combinations tested (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The recovery of GluA2 is unaffected by γ2.
source: Previous reports have shown that the recovery of GluA2 is unaffected by γ2 (Cais et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Recovery from desensitization was significantly slowed in the 2T(A2) receptor.
source: Interestingly, we found that recovery from desensitization was significantly slowed in the 2T(A2) receptor (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: AMPAR efficiency to the partial agonist kainate is enhanced as the number of TARPs in the AMPAR complex increase.
source: A previous study revealed that AMPAR efficiency to the partial agonist kainate is enhanced as the number of TARPs in the AMPAR complex increase (Shi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: TARP γ2 modified the percentage of perampanel block only when attached to GluA4c subunit.
source: The outcome of those experiments did show the same pattern as the one found for desensitization: TARP γ2 modified the percentage of block only when attached to GluA4c subunit.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data.

claim: CI-AMPARs with 2 TARPs at the GluA2 subunit displayed a similar perampanel block as TARPless CI-AMPARs.
source: CI-AMPARs with 2 TARPs at the GluA2 subunit displayed a similar block as TARPless CI-AMPARs (47.33 ± 5.95% for 0T vs. 46.13 ± 5.47% for 2T(A2); p>0.05; n = 6 and 5, respectively; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The block by perampanel in a 2-TARPed at GluA4c and in a 4-TARPed CI-AMPARs was higher than for TARPless receptors.
source: However, the block by perampanel in a 2-TARPed at GluA4c (70.65 ± 8.06; n = 7) and in a 4-TARPed CI-AMPARs (71.64 ± 6.76; n = 6) was higher than for TARPless receptors (p<0.05 for 0T vs. 2T(A4c) and 0T vs. 4T).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data.

claim: The CL mutation in the first TM domain of AMPAR subunit does not interfere with the binding of both proteins but prevents γ2 from modulating the kinetics of AMPARs.
source: This point mutation in the first TM domain of AMPAR subunit does not interfere with the binding of both proteins but prevents γ2 from modulating the kinetics of AMPARs.
evidence: This is based on prior work cited in the manuscript (Hawken et al., 2017).

claim: The slowing of desensitization kinetics caused by γ2 was prevented in the C550L mutated GluA4c receptor.
source: When we compared responses from cells transfected with either GluA4c:γ2 or GluA4c(C550L):γ2, we confirmed that the slowing of desensitization kinetics caused by γ2 was prevented in the C550L mutated receptor (6.31 ± 0.80 ms for GluA4c:γ2 vs. 3.60 ± 0.60 ms for GluA4c(C550L):γ2; p=0.036; student's t-test; n = 11 and 6, respectively; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The CL mutation had a dampening effect on single channel conductance modulation, avoiding the typical increase induced by γ2.
source: Moreover, we expanded the previously described CL mutation blunting effects by observing that it had also a dampening effect on single channel conductance modulation, avoiding the typical increase induced by γ2 (Soto et al., 2007) (23.84 ± 1.87 pS for GluA4c:γ2 vs. 17.46 ± 2.99 pS for GluA4c(C550L):γ2; p=0.031; student's t-test; n = 10 and 6, respectively; Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2, with citation to prior work.

claim: The blunting C550L mutation did not prevent the slowing of kinetics caused by γ2 attached to GluA4c in CI-AMPARs.
source: The blunting C550L mutation did not prevent the slowing of kinetics caused by γ2 attached to GluA4c (p=0.9189; student's t-test; n = 21 and 12, respectively; Figure 6—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The milder increase in conductance caused by γ2 when it is attached to GluA4c was avoided by the C550L mutation and conductance levels were very similar to the ones seen in TARPless condition.
source: However, the milder increase in conductance caused by γ2 when it is attached to GluA4c (9.72 ± 1.09 pS – 2T(A4c)) was avoided and conductance levels were very similar to the ones seen in TARPless condition (6.03 ± 0.63 pS in 2T(A4c(550L)) vs. 5.15 ± 0.50 pS in 0T; p=0.2775; Figure 6—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The C549L mutation on GluA2 did not affect the increase in conductance caused by γ2 when it is linked to GluA2.
source: Surprisingly, the C549L mutation on GluA2 did not affect the increase in conductance caused by γ2 when it is linked to GluA2 (p=0.8556; student's t-test; n = 10 and 6, respectively; Figure 6—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: CGCs have a high expression of GluA2 and GluA4c AMPAR subunits.
source: CGCs have a high expression of GluA2 and GluA4c AMPAR subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CGC expression patterns.

claim: CGCs only express two TARPs (γ2 and γ7).
source: Besides, these neurons only express two TARPs (γ2 and γ7) (Fukaya et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: No other auxiliary subunits such as cornichons have been described to be functionally present in CGCs.
source: and no other auxiliary subunits such as cornichons have been described to be functionally present.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding CGC auxiliary subunits.

claim: γ2 has been proved to be essential in AMPAR signalling in CGCs.
source: While γ2 has been proved to be essential in AMPAR signalling in this cell type (Chen et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The role of γ7 does not seem to be important to determine CI-AMPAR expression in granule cells.
source: the role of γ7 does not seem to be important to determine CI-AMPAR expression in granule cells (Studniarczyk et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Values obtained from CGCs were closely equivalent to values from recombinant receptors only for a 2-TARPed CI-AMPAR with the two TARP molecules linked to the GluA2 subunit.
source: Taken together, it was clear that values obtained from CGCs were closely equivalent to values from recombinant receptors only for a 2-TARPed CI-AMPAR with the two TARP molecules linked to the GluA2 subunit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing experimental data from CGCs with recombinant systems.

claim: CGCs somatic patches showed an exceptionally slow recovery from desensitization that was different from any CI-AMPAR studied.
source: Surprisingly, we consistently recorded currents with an exceptionally slow recovery that were different from any CI-AMPAR studied (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: No resensitization of the receptors was observed in CGC somatic patches during prolonged AMPA application, ruling out any contribution of γ7 to CI-AMPAR currents from somatic CGCs.
source: We did not appreciate any change in desensitized current in the presence of the agonist for the whole recording period (Figure 7J) ruling out any contribution of γ7 to CI-AMPAR currents from somatic CGCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Recordings from cell lines expressing GluA2:γ2+GluA4c did not vary when AMPA was used as agonist compared to glutamate.
source: However, recordings from cell lines expressing GluA2:γ2+GluA4c did not vary when we used AMPA as agonist (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), ruling out this possibility.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: CI-AMPARs from somatic CGCs are very possibly modulated by two γ2 in a similar manner as in the 2T(A2) condition.
source: All together, these results seem to indicate that CI-AMPARs from somatic CGCs are very possibly modulated by two γ2 in a similar manner as in our 2T(A2) condition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: mEPSCs were differentially altered depending on the TARP expression levels.
source: One of the first evidences of a functionally variable AMPAR-TARP stoichiometry came from the observation that mEPSCs were differentially altered depending on the TARP expression levels (Milstein et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The pharmacology – the kainate efficacy – of recombinant AMPARs was stoichiometry-dependent.
source: Shortly after, by using fusion constructs similar to the ones used in our study it was seen that the pharmacology – the kainate efficacy – of recombinant AMPARs was stoichiometry-dependent (Shi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: AMPARs from hippocampal pyramidal and dentate gyrus granule neurons were 4 and 2-TARPed, respectively.
source: This same work suggested that AMPARs from hippocampal pyramidal and dentate gyrus granule neurons were 4 and 2-TARPed, respectively.
evidence: This is based on prior work, as indicated by the context.

claim: A recent work has provided evidence for the presence of different stoichiometries in cerebellar cells – 2 and 4 TARPed AMPARs in stellate and Purkinje cells, respectively.
source: Finally, a recent work has provided evidence for the presence of different stoichiometries in cerebellar cells – 2 and 4 TARPed AMPARs in stellate and Purkinje cells, respectively (Dawe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A full TARPed GluA1 receptor is necessary to vary CP-AMPAR single channel conductance.
source: However, a more intricate modulation appears to be present since a full TARPed GluA1 receptor is necessary to vary other CP-AMPAR intrinsic properties such as single channel conductance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's experimental data.

claim: Open probability and rise time are not altered by the number of TARPs acting on AMPARs.
source: On the other hand, other characteristics are not altered by the number of TARPs acting on AMPARs (open probability or rise time).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's experimental data.

claim: Ib TARPs (γ4 and γ8) seem to associate with AMPARs in a 2-TARPed dependent manner.
source: It might be interesting in the future to test whether other auxiliary subunits from the TARP family modulate the AMPAR features studied here, especially single channel conductance since Ib TARPs (γ4 and γ8) seem to associate with AMPARs in a 2-TARPed dependent manner (Hastie et al., 2013; Herguedas et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ib TARPs clearly produce an increase in AMPAR channel conductance.
source: although they clearly produce an increase in AMPAR channel conductance (Shi et al., 2010; Suzuki et al., 2008; Soto et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: For GluA1, only TARPs γ4 and γ8 are able to increase the period of time to the peak response.
source: In line with that, for this same homomeric AMPAR it has been shown in HEK cells that only TARPs γ4 and γ8 are able to increase the period of time to the peak response (Milstein et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: mEPSCs recordings from CGCs have revealed no differences in the rise time of these quantal synaptic currents when the 'dose' of TARP γ2 was altered into the receptor by using homozygous or heterozygous stargazer mice.
source: Previous mEPSCs recordings from CGCs, which are mediated by CI-AMPARs have revealed no differences in the rise time of these quantal synaptic currents when the 'dose' of TARP γ2 was altered into the receptor by using homozygous or heterozygous stargazer mice (Milstein et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The overexpression of TARP γ2 in CGCs increased kainate affinity.
source: In fact, the overexpression of TARP γ2 in this cell type increased kainate affinity (Milstein et al., 2007), indicating that CGCs are not totally saturated by TARPs since the efficiency to kainate is strongly dependent on the number of TARPs in the complex (Shi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CGCs are not totally saturated by TARPs.
source: In fact, the overexpression of TARP γ2 in this cell type increased kainate affinity (Milstein et al., 2007), indicating that CGCs are not totally saturated by TARPs since the efficiency to kainate is strongly dependent on the number of TARPs in the complex (Shi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited prior work.

claim: TARP subtypes might have different binding sites in the AMPAR complex.
source: It has been suggested that TARP subtypes might have different binding sites in the AMPAR complex (Greger et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Only two γ4 can co-assemble with AMPARs as seen with single-molecule photobleaching in live cells.
source: on the basis that, for example, only two γ4 can co-assemble with AMPARs as seen with single-molecule photobleaching in live cells (Hastie et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Hippocampal CA1 neurons express almost exclusively heteromeric CI-AMPARs.
source: Hippocampal CA1 neurons express almost exclusively heteromeric CI-AMPARs (Wenthold et al., 1996; Lu et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Hippocampal CA1 neurons present a 2-TARPs stoichiometry together with 2 CNIHs.
source: and present a 2-TARPs stoichiometry together with 2 CNIHs (Gill et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In CGCs, γ7 could potentially be playing a role at somatic AMPARs although it has been shown to selectively suppress somatic CI-AMPARs in CGCs.
source: However, in CGCs, γ7 could potentially be playing a role at somatic AMPARs although it has been shown to selectively suppress somatic CI-AMPARs in CGCs (Studniarczyk et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: γ7 does not have an important involvement in excitatory transmission in CGCs.
source: and not to have an important involvement in excitatory transmission (Yamazaki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Resensitization is a fingerprint that indicates the presence of 4-TARPed AMPARs.
source: However, resensitization is a fingerprint that indicates the presence of 4-TARPed AMPARs (Kato et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Purkinje cells from stargazer mice, with low γ7 stoichiometry lack resensitization.
source: Indeed, Purkinje cells from stargazer mice, with low γ7 stoichiometry lack this feature (Gill et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The absence of resensitization reinforces the view of a 2-TARPed conformation in CGCs.
source: Thus, the absence of resensitization, a characteristic signature of a fully TARPed receptor, reinforces the view of a 2-TARPed conformation in CGCs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and prior knowledge.

claim: AMPA is known to speed entry into desensitization and to slow recovery, relative to glutamate.
source: The use of AMPA as agonist in CGC experiments to circumvent other glutamate-activated receptors – especially kainate receptors present in CGCs (Bahn et al., 1994; Belcher and Howe, 1997) – might account for the slow recovery since this agonist is known to speed entry into desensitization and to slow recovery, relative to glutamate (Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: An inverse relationship between the affinity of the agonist and recovery from AMPAR desensitization exists in the absence of TARPs.
source: In the absence of TARPs, it has been demonstrated that an inverse relationship between the affinity of the agonist and recovery from AMPAR desensitization exist (Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: γ2 causes a drastic reorganization of the AMPAR complex.
source: As seen in many studies, γ2 causes a drastic reorganization of the complex
evidence: This is established knowledge from multiple studies.

claim: A well-known consequence of the presence of γ2 is the increased affinity of the receptor for glutamate.
source: and a well-known consequence of the presence of γ2 is the increased affinity of the receptor for glutamate (Priel et al., 2005; Tomita et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Similar channel conductance estimates were reported, regardless of the use of AMPA or glutamate as agonist.
source: Similar channel conductance estimates were reported, regardless of the use of AMPA or glutamate as agonist (Swanson et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: For GluA2/GluA4, similar conductance values have been described for both AMPA and glutamate agonists (5.5–6 pS).
source: Furthermore, for GluA2/GluA4, similar conductance values have been described for both agonists (5.5–6 pS) (Swanson et al., 1997), matching the values obtained in our and other studies (Jackson et al., 2011) using the agonist glutamate.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The kinetic properties of AMPA-activated GluA4 homomers were comparable to those activated by glutamate.
source: Conversely, in our hands, AMPAR desensitization kinetics of GluA4c seemed to be significantly slower when AMPA was used as agonist (data not shown) despite previous reports indicating that the kinetic properties of AMPA-activated GluA4 homomers were comparable to those activated by glutamate (Swanson et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Recovery from desensitization is strongly reduced either in neurons and heteromeric recombinant AMPARs by the members of the CKAMP family.
source: The remarkably slow recovery of the currents in CGCs could be also attributed to the presence of CKAMPs in the native AMPAR complex since recovery from desensitization is strongly reduced either in neurons and heteromeric recombinant AMPARs by the members of the CKAMP family (Farrow et al., 2015; von Engelhardt et al., 2010; Klaassen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CKAMP39 is highly expressed in the cerebellum.
source: Notably, one of the members of the family, CKAMP39, is highly expressed in the cerebellum (Farrow et al., 2015; von Engelhardt, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There is really low expression of GSG1L and CKAMP44 (shisa9) in CGCs.
source: Considering the reported absence of other members of the TARP family in CGCs, the functional absence of CNIH2 (Shi et al., 2010) and the really low expression of other AMPAR auxiliary proteins as GSG1L and CKAMP44 (shisa9) (Zeisel et al., 2018), CKAMP39 might be a potential good candidate.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: AMPAR responses depend on the subunit composition but also importantly rely on the nature of the auxiliary subunit/s accompanying them.
source: AMPAR responses depend on the subunit composition but also importantly rely on the nature of the auxiliary subunit/s accompanying them.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study and established knowledge.

claim: AMPAR properties can be modulated differently depending on the number of TARPs, the type of AMPAR and the specific interactions that these auxiliary subunits set up with a given GluA subunit.
source: This work adds important information about the extraordinary degree of functional variety in AMPARs and shows that AMPAR properties can be modulated differently depending on the number of TARPs, the type of AMPAR and the specific interactions that these auxiliary subunits set up with a given GluA subunit.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the study's experimental data.

claim: The broad number of possible combinations of pore-forming plus auxiliary subunits and stoichiometries that can be achieved on AMPARs generate a profuse diversity in glutamatergic responses in the brain.
source: The broad number of possible combinations of pore-forming plus auxiliary subunits and stoichiometries that can be achieved on AMPARs generate a profuse diversity in glutamatergic responses in the brain.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study's findings and established knowledge.
